deep.reconstruction:
Context: this is p. 25 of Riemann's 1851 doctoral dissertation, "Grundlagen für eine allgemeine Theorie der Functionen einer veränderlichen complexen Grösse". The page finishes Art. 16 and contains all of Art. 17. This is the existence part of what Riemann later (1857) named the Dirichlet principle.

(A) End of Art. 16.
Goal: λ cannot approach a function γ that jumps along a curve while L = ∫(λ_x² + λ_y²) dT stays bounded.

Setting from the previous page:
- Use normal coordinates (s, p) along the discontinuity curve, with curvature κ.
- The strip T' is bounded by p = p1(s) > 0 and p = p2(s) < 0.
- The boundary values there are γ1 and γ2.
- The strip's contribution to L is at least ∫ (γ1−γ2)² κ ds / D(p1,p2), where D = log(1−κ p2) − log(1−κ p1).
- This bound is the minimum of ∫_{p2}^{p1} λ_p² (1−κp) dp with fixed end values. [mine] The Euler–Lagrange equation ((1−κp) λ')' = 0 gives λ' = c/(1−κp), hence the minimum (γ1−γ2)² κ / D.
- Fix reference widths P1, P2.
- m(s) is chosen so that, however thin the strip, there are admissible p1, p2 with (γ1−γ2)² > m.
- Set a = ∫ m κ ds / D(P1,P2).

This page: choose p1 < (1 − (1−κP1)^{a/C})/κ and p2 > (1 − (1−κP2)^{a/C})/κ, together with (γ1−γ2)² > m.

[mine] The first condition gives 1−κp1 > (1−κP1)^{a/C}, so log(1−κp1) > (a/C) log(1−κP1). Likewise log(1−κp2) < (a/C) log(1−κP2). Hence 0 < D(p1,p2) < (a/C) D(P1,P2).

Therefore ∫ (γ1−γ2)² κ ds / D(p1,p2) > (C/a) ∫ m κ ds / D(P1,P2) = C. So the part of L coming from this piece of T', and a fortiori L itself, exceeds C for every λ. As C → ∞, a/C → 0, so p1, p2 → 0 and the strip can be taken arbitrarily thin. Q.E.D.

(B) Art. 17.
Art. 15 gives the vanishing of the first variation of Ω at the minimiser u:
N = ∫_T [(u_x − β_y) λ_x + (u_y + β_x) λ_y] dT = 0 for every admissible λ (λ = 0 on the boundary, finite L).

Step 1 (Green's theorem). Remove small pieces T' around the singularities of u, β, λ; call the rest T''. Apply Art. 7, ∫(X_x + Y_y) dT = −∫(X x_p + Y y_p) ds with p the inner normal, to X = (u_x − β_y) λ and Y = (u_y + β_x) λ.
- [mine] X_x + Y_y = λ Δu + [(u_x−β_y) λ_x + (u_y+β_x) λ_y], because the mixed derivatives of β cancel.
- [mine] Using x_p = y_s and y_p = −x_s, the boundary integrand becomes λ (u_p − β_s).
- So the T''-part of N is −∫ λ Δu dT − ∫ (u_p − β_s) λ ds.
- On the outer boundary λ = 0, so only the boundaries of the pieces T' contribute.
- Hence N = −∫_{T''} λ Δu dT + {∫_{T'} [...] dT + ∫_{∂T'} (u_p − β_s) λ ds}.

Step 2. Suppose Δu ≠ 0 somewhere. Take λ = 0 in T' and of the same sign as Δu in T''. Then N ≠ 0, a contradiction. So Δu = 0 throughout, and then the singular contributions must also vanish.

Step 3. Put X = u_x − β_y and Y = u_y + β_x. Then X_x + Y_y = 0, and the flux ∫(X x_p + Y y_p) ds = ∫(u_p − β_s) ds vanishes over the boundary of every part of T (even around singular points).

Step 4. Cut T by cross-cuts (Art. 9) into a simply connected T*.
- σ(O) = ∫_{O0}^{O} (u_p − β_s) ds is then path-independent.
- σ is continuous in T* and jumps by the same constant on both sides of each cut.
- [mine] dσ = X dy − Y dx.
- Then v = β + σ satisfies v_x = −u_y and v_y = u_x (Cauchy–Riemann).

Theorem (Lehrsatz). If α + βi is given on T with ∫[(α_x − β_y)² + (α_y + β_x)²] dT finite, it can be turned into an analytic function u + vi of z by adding a complex quantity that:
- is purely imaginary on the boundary;
- is continuous in T* except at isolated points;
- jumps across the cuts by imaginary constants.
The statement continues on the next page.
errors: No computational errors. The choice of p1, p2 does give log(1−κp2) − log(1−κp1) < (a/C)·[log(1−κP2) − log(1−κP1)], and the bound > C follows; the case κ < 0 works the same way, and κ = 0 is the limit.
Art. 16 tacitly assumes 1 − κp > 0 on the strip and a piecewise smooth discontinuity curve. It also needs m(s) chosen measurably, with ∫ m κ ds / D finite and positive; this is only sketched.

Art. 17 assumes the minimiser u has continuous second derivatives off isolated points, so that Green's theorem gives −∫λΔu. Deriving harmonicity from the weak equation N = 0 needs a regularity result (Weyl's lemma, 1940), which Riemann does not supply.
The whole argument rests on Art. 15's unproved assumption that Ω attains its minimum. This is Weierstrass's 1870 objection, later repaired by Hilbert (1900/1904); it is not a slip on this page.

results.what: Lower bound for the Dirichlet energy across a thin curved strip, via the 1-D minimiser ∫λ'²(1−κp)dp ≥ (Δγ)²κ / log((1−κp2)/(1−κp1)). It shows finite-energy functions cannot approximate functions with jump discontinuities along curves.
results.modern_name: Capacity/energy estimate; H^1 functions have no jumps across curves (trace argument)

results.what: Vanishing first variation plus Green's theorem implies Δu = 0 (Euler–Lagrange equation of the Dirichlet integral), and the flux of (X, Y) vanishes around singular points.
results.modern_name: Euler–Lagrange equation for the Dirichlet integral (classical form of the weak Laplace equation)

results.what: Construction of the harmonic conjugate v = β + ∫(u_p − β_s)ds on the cut, simply connected surface T*, with constant periods across cross-cuts.
results.modern_name: Harmonic conjugate / periods of a closed differential on a multiply connected domain

results.what: Lehrsatz: any α + βi with finite ∫[(α_x−β_y)² + (α_y+β_x)²] can be made analytic by adding a function that is imaginary on the boundary (with prescribed jump structure).
results.modern_name: Dirichlet principle / existence theorem for analytic functions with given real boundary values

deep.surprise_reason: This page is the text of Riemann's published 1851 dissertation (end of Art. 16 and Art. 17), the well-known Dirichlet-principle existence theorem; it is fully published and credited to him.
